title: How every prequalification network works (shared model)
body:
All contractor prequalification networks (ISNetworld, Avetta, Veriforce/PEC, BROWZ, ComplyWorks) sit between a hiring client (operator/GC/owner) and a contractor. Consistent pattern: the CONTRACTOR pays; the HIRING CLIENT mandates which platform. You do not choose your platform — your client dictates it. A contractor working for operators on ISN, Avetta and Veriforce must maintain three separate, non-portable profiles; being compliant on one gives zero credit on another.

Reviewers never see crews work. They see uploaded insurance certificates, written safety programs, OSHA logs, and questionnaire answers. Contractors almost never fail on safety PERFORMANCE — they fail on RECORDS that don't hold up to review. This is the single most important framing.

Three lagging indicators follow a contractor everywhere for ~3 years: TRIR (Total Recordable Incident Rate), DART (Days Away/Restricted/Transferred), and EMR (Experience Modification Rate). Most oil & gas / industrial operators set thresholds at 1.0 or lower for TRIR and EMR. One bad year affects the grade for up to 36 months.

Cross-checking is universal: reported TRIR must reconcile with OSHA 300/300A logs; questionnaire answers must match uploaded documents; training claims must match individual completion records. Every mismatch triggers a corrective cycle (rejection -> fix -> resubmit -> re-review).

"Certification" is a misnomer on all of these — there is no universal "Avetta certification" or "Veriforce certification." You are COMPLIANT FOR A SPECIFIC HIRING CLIENT, not certified by the platform. Requirements are client-configured.

Market consolidation: BROWZ -> Avetta (2019). PICS Auditing -> Avetta. PEC Safety <-> Veriforce (merged 2019). ComplyWorks -> Veriforce (2020). Today there are effectively THREE networks: ISNetworld, Avetta, and Veriforce (carrying PEC and ComplyWorks brands).

title: ISNetworld (ISN) — what it is and who uses it
body:
ISNetworld (ISN), by ISN Software Corp, is the dominant contractor prequalification platform in oil & gas, refining, petrochemical, heavy manufacturing, and broad energy. Hiring clients invite contractors to connect; the contractor pays an annual subscription (tiered by employee count, roughly $875-$2,000+). Compliance is evaluated per hiring client and expressed as a standardized 0-100 grade per client. Common minimum thresholds are 70-80 depending on the operator.

ISN's two review services are RAVS (Review & Verification Services) for written safety programs and I-RAVS for insurance. The MSQ (Management System Questionnaire) is a very long questionnaire (800-2,000 questions) that drives part of the grade.

title: How ISN grades a contractor (A/B/C/F, per-client weighting)
body:
ISN produces a standardized 0-100 grade shown per hiring client, often mapped to letters A/B/C/F. Each client sets its own weighting and passing threshold (commonly 70-80). The grade is a weighted blend of, roughly: RAVS written-program review (~30-40%), TRIR (~30%), DART (~20%), MSQ questionnaire (10-15%), EMR (10-15%), and OSHA citation history (10-20%). Exact weights are client-configured and not published — treat these as directional.

Because grading is per-client and continuous, a certificate expiring or a metric updating can move the grade with nobody touching the account. TRIR/DART are recalculated from the OSHA 300 data the contractor enters and must reconcile with the uploaded 300/300A logs.

title: How ISN RAVS reviews a written safety program (content, not format)
body:
RAVS (Review & Verification Services) is a human review of the contractor's written safety programs against a checklist of required elements per topic. THE CRITICAL RULE: RAVS is a CONTENT check, not a format check — "if a required element is not literally on the page, it counts as missing." Reviewers go element-by-element; a program that alludes to a requirement but does not state it explicitly is marked deficient.

Each written program must, for its topic, contain: the specific procedure, NAMED responsible parties (title/role, not "management"), inspection/audit FREQUENCIES, training requirements (who, by whom, how often, how documented), recordkeeping and retention, and the governing OSHA citation. Programs must be company-specific — assertive ("{Company} WILL...") not conditional ("employees should when possible"), dated, and reflect the contractor's actual scope of work.
rejection_reasons: Required element not literally stated on the page (counts as missing even if implied)
Generic/template manual that could belong to any company
Responsibilities vague ('management is responsible') instead of named roles
Missing training frequency or documentation method
Non-assertive language ('should', 'when possible') instead of 'will/shall'
Program undated or not reflecting actual scope of work

title: ISN/RAVS rejection reasons — the concrete list
body:
The most common reasons a RAVS submission is returned "not accepted":
- Company-specificity / template failure: manual reads as a generic template, not this company's program.
- Missing elements: e.g. a Confined Space program with no rescue plan; LOTO without periodic inspection; Fall Protection without a competent-person designation.
- Responsibility gaps: no named person/role accountable for the program.
- Training gaps: frequency not stated, or no method of documentation.
- Citation problems: wrong or missing OSHA citation for the topic.
- Non-assertive language: "should"/"may"/"when feasible" instead of committed "will/shall".
- Dating: program undated or clearly stale.
- I-RAVS insurance triggers: COI limits/endorsements below the client's requirement, missing additional-insured or waiver of subrogation, EMR letter from broker not carrier.
- Q&A / statistics triggers: MSQ answers or entered TRIR/DART that contradict the uploaded 300/300A logs.
rejection_reasons: Template/generic manual (not company-specific)
Confined space program missing a rescue plan
LOTO missing periodic (annual) inspection procedure
Fall protection missing competent-person designation
No named responsible party for the program
Training frequency or documentation method missing
Wrong or missing OSHA citation
Non-assertive language instead of will/shall
Undated or stale program
COI limits/endorsements below client requirement (I-RAVS)
EMR letter from broker instead of carrier
Entered TRIR/DART contradicts uploaded OSHA 300/300A

title: ISN I-RAVS — insurance certificate review
body: I-RAVS is ISN's insurance verification service. Reviewers check each uploaded COI against the hiring client's configured requirements: coverage types (GL, Workers' Comp, Auto, Umbrella/Excess), per-occurrence and aggregate LIMITS, additional-insured endorsement (CG 20 10 / CG 20 37 or equivalent), blanket waiver of subrogation, primary & non-contributory wording, named insured EXACTLY matching the ISN registration, and effective dates preceding work start. EMR must be supported by a letter issued by the insurance CARRIER stating the current rate — a broker summary or premium statement is rejected.
rejection_reasons: COI limits below the client's required limits
Missing additional-insured endorsement
Missing blanket waiver of subrogation
Named insured doesn't match ISN registration exactly
Effective dates after work start
EMR letter from broker not carrier

title: ISN RAVS variants: T-RAVS, I-RAVS, RAVS Plus/360, MSQ
body:
RAVS family:
- RAVS: written safety-program content review.
- T-RAVS: training verification (individual employee training completion records).
- I-RAVS: insurance/COI review.
- RAVS Plus / RAVS 360: field verification — an on-site or evidence-based check that programs are actually implemented (inspection records, closed corrective actions, training rosters), not just written.
- MSQ (Management System Questionnaire): 800-2,000 question self-assessment of the contractor's safety management system; answers must be consistent with uploaded documents and metrics.

title: Avetta (incl. BROWZ, PICS) — what it is and who uses it
body: Avetta is a global supply-chain risk-management and contractor prequalification platform built from PICS Auditing + BROWZ (BROWZ fully migrated into Avetta by end of 2020). Strongest in construction/GC, utilities, facilities management, manufacturing, telecom, healthcare, and general industry — broader and less oil-&-gas-centric than ISN, and global. Hiring client "connects" the contractor; contractor pays to register and keep documents current. Compliance is evaluated per hiring client. Fees are quoted at signup and driven by risk level, employee count, and number of client connections (small firms ~$450-$900/yr; larger up to ~$3,499-$4,999+). Avetta bills partly by client connections and has been reported to auto-charge when a new client connects a contractor.

title: How Avetta scores contractors (traffic-light flag + Safety Maturity Index)
body:
Avetta uses two related systems.

(a) Compliance status — a per-client traffic-light flag:
- GREEN = Compliant: every client-configured requirement met; bid-eligible.
- AMBER = Conditional/Warning: minor variance or upcoming expiration (e.g., COI inside its 30-day expiration window); usually still allowed to work but "on a clock."
- RED = Non-Compliant: critical failure (failed safety-manual audit, expired OSHA logs, EMR/TRIR over cap, missed annual update); disqualified for that client.
The flag is per-client and moves on its own; grades update near real-time. Avetta scores against a client-specific threshold that can change without notice — many large GCs require 70+, tier-one clients 80+.

(b) Safety Maturity Index (SMI): a separate NSC-developed 0-100 predictive score across five SMS categories, graded A (76-100)/B (51-75)/C (26-50)/D (0-25), weighted by evidence verification level (Self-Attestation lowest -> Evidence of SMS Practice -> Digital SMS Quality & Usage highest). SMI is a leading-indicator layer on top of prequalification, not the pass/fail gate.

title: Avetta Safety Manual Audit (DocuGUARD / InsureGUARD)
body: Avetta's equivalent to ISN's RAVS is the Safety Manual Audit, delivered via document modules branded DocuGUARD (documents) and InsureGUARD (insurance). It is a third-party HUMAN review of written safety programs against regulatory and client-specific requirements — reviewers read the content, not just that a file exists. Reviewers increasingly demand PROOF OF IMPLEMENTATION (inspection records, per-employee training completions, closed corrective actions), not just written policy. First submissions are commonly returned "Review & Resubmit"; turnaround ~1-2 weeks per cycle, registration commonly 30-45 days.

title: Avetta rejection / flag reasons — the concrete list
body:
Avetta rejection/flag reasons:
- Generic/template safety manuals (the #1 audit failure) — reviewers want procedure-level specificity: named responsible parties, inspection frequencies, step-by-step procedures for the programs your trade actually requires.
- Programs not updated after an OSHA standard revision.
- OSHA 300/300A logs that don't reconcile with reported rates (especially hours-worked miscalculation).
- EMR letter from a broker instead of the carrier.
- EMR/TRIR over the client's cap (common hard cutoffs 1.0 or 1.25; can auto-filter with no manual review).
- Insurance/COI defects: expired; auto-renewal with different limits; endorsement wording no longer matching; missing additional-insured (CG 20 10) or blanket waiver of subrogation; named insured not matching registration exactly; effective dates after work start.
- Citation with no documented corrective action.
- Missing/incomplete uploads (90% complete still holds status down).
- Questionnaire answers contradicting attached documents.
- No internal account owner monitoring alerts/renewals.
- Expired credentials on review (e.g., superintendent's OSHA 30 lapsed).

Program not updated after OSHA standard revision
OSHA 300/300A don't reconcile with reported rates (hours-worked error)
EMR letter from broker instead of carrier
EMR/TRIR over client cap (1.0/1.25)
COI expired / wrong limits / missing additional-insured or waiver
Named insured not matching registration exactly
Citation with no documented corrective action
Missing/incomplete required uploads
Questionnaire answers contradict attached documents
No internal account owner monitoring status
Expired credentials (e.g., lapsed OSHA 30)

title: Veriforce (incl. PEC, ComplyWorks) — what it is and who uses it
body: Veriforce is a contractor prequalification, safety, training, and Operator Qualification (OQ) platform, strongest in pipeline, midstream, oil & gas, and utilities — especially DOT-regulated pipeline work (49 CFR 192/195). In 2019 PEC Safety and Veriforce merged into one company under the Veriforce brand (~350 hiring clients, 25,000 contractor companies, 400+ training courses). Model is operator-driven with per-operator thresholds. Contractor-Management subscription is tiered by employee count (~$500-$5,000+/yr; mid-size GCs $1,500-$5,000). Operator Qualification is a SEPARATE subscription: ~$250 one-time setup, then priced per QI (Qualified Individual), roughly $179-$220/QI/yr with a DOT bundle tiered by QI count. Verify pricing against a live quote — it drifts.

title: How Veriforce scores contractors (per-operator; A-F letter grades)
body:
Veriforce is not a single pass/fail and does not publish its algorithm. Operators evaluate profiles using lagging indicators, documentation completeness, and program specificity; scoring is per-operator (same docs can grade differently across operators). Display formats a hiring client can choose:
- Compliant / Not Compliant
- Color: Green (good standing) / Yellow (mitigation plan required) / Red (not allowed to work)
- Letter A-F: A or B = approved; C, D, or F = unapproved, requiring an exception or mitigation.
Primary lagging indicators: TRIR and EMR benchmarked against BLS averages for the contractor's NAICS/trade; thresholds commonly 1.0 or lower. Being over-threshold isn't always fatal if a documented corrective-action plan is provided — a high rate with NO explanation is what's fatal. Status is live to operators; expired documents flag automatically and can remove a contractor from an approved vendor list without advance warning.

title: Veriforce T-RAVS written-program review + field assessments + OQ
body: Veriforce's written-program review is branded T-RAVS (aligned to the contractor's scope of work) — a human document review; contractors upload written programs covering the OSHA topics relevant to their scope, graded against a checklist. Veriforce also runs regulatory FIELD ASSESSMENTS/audits for OQ and Drug & Alcohol program IMPLEMENTATION (on-site interviews + documentation review). The distinctive Veriforce layer is Operator Qualification (OQ): proof that the INDIVIDUAL performing a DOT-covered task has been evaluated and qualified for it — per individual, per covered task, with completion dates. PEC Safety Training (PEC Core / PEC Basic Orientation) via Veriforce Learn is a common site-access prerequisite on pipeline/oilfield/utility clients.

title: Veriforce / PEC rejection / flag reasons — the concrete list
body:
Veriforce/PEC rejection/flag reasons:
- Generic compliance language instead of documented procedures ("we follow all applicable OSHA requirements" fails T-RAVS).
- Program doesn't match work scope (polished but unrealistic tasks/wrong hazards — a frequent flag for un-validated AI-generated content).
- Vague roles/accountability ("management is responsible") — reviewers want who, what authority, stop-work authority, escalation paths.
- Weak training/competency systems: training that exists only as a sign-in sheet with no assessment or competency evaluation.
- Training records missing individual employee names or completion dates.
- OQ records at the company level instead of individual worker + task level.
- OSHA 300 logs that don't reconcile with reported TRIR.
- TRIR/EMR over threshold with no documented corrective-action plan.
- Expired insurance certificates not renewed in the portal.
- Missing Drug & Alcohol program documentation (DOT context).
- Operator questionnaires answered vaguely; poor responses to manual-audit flags.
- Missing incident/case-management process (reportable incidents, investigation, tracked/closed corrective actions).

Program doesn't match actual work scope (wrong hazards/tasks)
Vague roles/accountability (no named person, authority, stop-work)
Training is sign-in sheets only, no competency assessment
Training records missing individual names or dates
OQ records at company level, not per individual + covered task
OSHA 300 doesn't reconcile with reported TRIR
TRIR/EMR over threshold with no corrective-action plan
Expired insurance not renewed in portal
Missing Drug & Alcohol program documentation
Vague questionnaire answers / poor responses to audit flags
Missing incident/case-management process

title: PEC (now inside Veriforce) — Premier, SSQ, Core, Basic Orientation
body: PEC Safety is no longer a separate live platform — it merged with Veriforce in 2019. PEC Premier is the legacy prequalification product: vets contractors via the PEC Standardized Safety Questionnaire (SSQ) plus compliance metrics; historically strong with independent oil & gas operators in the Gulf of Mexico. PEC Basic Orientation and PEC Core Compliance are widely-accepted worker training programs, now under Veriforce Learn. If a client references "PEC," "PEC Premier," "PEC Core," or "SSQ," route them to Veriforce — same ecosystem post-2019. Grading/rejection logic mirrors Veriforce.

title: BROWZ (absorbed into Avetta) — route to Avetta
body: BROWZ no longer exists as a standalone platform. Avetta and BROWZ combined (announced Feb 14, 2019); by end of 2020 all BROWZ clients migrated to Avetta. BROWZ login, scores, and RAVS-style uploads now live inside Avetta. BROWZ historically served mining, transportation, construction, chemicals, aerospace, pharmaceuticals, energy, utilities as a comparatively straightforward document-collection portal. If a bid packet still says "BROWZ compliance required" (still common in Permian/DFW/Texas RFQs), the client simply hasn't updated their template — the requirement now routes through Avetta. There is no BROWZ account to create; grading/rejection logic = Avetta.

title: ComplyWorks (a Veriforce product) — Canada
body: ComplyWorks is a Canadian contractor compliance platform acquired by Veriforce Aug 18, 2020; it continues to operate under the ComplyWorks brand in Canada with largely unchanged document submission for Canadian contractors. Strongest in highly regulated Canadian sectors — oil & gas, property management, municipal operations, especially Western/West-Coast Canada. Canadian document nuances: WCB clearance letters (vs. US EMR), provincial requirements. Document review by the Veriforce/ComplyWorks team; scoring varies by hiring client. Grading/rejection logic mirrors Veriforce, plus Canada-specific items (missing/expired WCB/WorkSafe clearance letter, provincial requirement mismatches).
rejection_reasons: Missing/expired WCB (WorkSafe) clearance letter
Generic (non-scope-specific) written programs
Training records without individual names/dates or competency
Expired insurance not renewed in-portal
Provincial/regulatory requirement mismatches

title: Master cross-platform list: why submissions get rejected (ranked)
body:
Ranked by frequency across ISN, Avetta, Veriforce, BROWZ, ComplyWorks. Each is a DOCUMENTATION failure, not a safety failure:
1. Generic/template safety manual — no scope-specific procedures, no named responsible parties, no inspection frequencies (every platform's #1 program-review failure).
2. OSHA 300/300A logs that don't reconcile with reported TRIR/DART (especially hours-worked miscalculation).
3. Program-questionnaire-evidence contradictions.
4. Training records without individual names, completion dates, or competency verification (sign-in sheets only).
5. EMR provided as a broker summary rather than a carrier-issued EMR letter.
6. EMR/TRIR over the client's threshold with no documented corrective-action plan.
7. Insurance/COI defects — expired; wrong limits; missing additional-insured (CG 20 10); missing blanket waiver of subrogation; named insured not matching registration; effective dates after work start.
8. Citation with no attached corrective action.
9. Missing/incomplete required uploads (90% complete still holds status down).
10. OQ/covered-task records at company level instead of individual + task level (Veriforce/pipeline).
11. Missing Drug & Alcohol program documentation (Veriforce/DOT).
12. Program references outdated OSHA standards.
13. No internal account owner monitoring status, expirations, review flags.
14. Missing WCB/WorkSafe clearance letter (Canada/ComplyWorks).
15. AI-generated or over-committed programs describing tasks/hazards you don't actually have (scope-mismatch).

title: Key differences: ISN vs Avetta vs Veriforce (and what actually matters)
body:
ISNetworld: oil & gas / refining / heavy mfg; standardized 0-100 grade per client; written-program review = RAVS; insurance = I-RAVS; MSQ questionnaire; threshold ~70-80; fee ~$875-$2,000+.
Avetta (incl. BROWZ, PICS): construction/GC, utilities, facilities, global; traffic-light green/amber/red per client + separate SMI (A-D); review = Safety Manual Audit (DocuGUARD/InsureGUARD); threshold varies (~70+, tier-one 80+); fee ~$450-$900 small up to ~$3,499+.
Veriforce (incl. PEC, ComplyWorks): pipeline/midstream/DOT/utilities, Canada via ComplyWorks; per-operator thresholds, display Compliant/color/letter A-F (A/B approved); review = T-RAVS; distinctive OQ per individual/task + D&A + PEC training; fee ~$500-$5,000+ plus OQ per-QI.

What actually matters for advising a contractor:
1. You don't pick the platform — the client does. Get written confirmation of WHICH platform and WHAT minimum threshold before paying for anything.
2. One well-written, scope-specific program can satisfy all three — build it once (cite standards, name responsible parties, read as your own company).
3. The scoring engine is the same three numbers: TRIR, EMR, DART — rolling ~3-year averages benchmarked to BLS by NAICS. You can't fix this quarter's grade this quarter, so document corrective-action plans for any recordable that pushed you over 1.0.
4. Everything is continuous, not annual. COIs, EMR letters, training, OSHA logs move status automatically; treating any platform as once-a-year is the #1 cause of silent removal.
5. Passing prequal is not done — operators layer their own field verification (e.g., Chevron CHESM) checking that JSAs/inspections in the profile actually happen on site.
